info.bio:
Charles Hardin Holley (Lubbock, Texas, 7 de septiembre de 1936 - 3 de febrero de 1959), más conocido como Buddy Holly, fue un compositor y cantante estadounidense, uno de los más destacados pioneros del rock and roll.

Holley, en cuya familia había un gran interés por la música, aprendió a temprana edad a tocar el violín, el piano y la guitarra. En el otoño de 1949 conoció en el instituto Hutchinson Jr. a Bob Montgomery, con el que poco después formó el dúo "Buddy and Bob".

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

podcast.title: Decision to Pursue Rock and Roll (1955)
podcast.body: Buddy Holly decided he wanted to be a rock and roll star after seeing Elvis live in 1955. The promoter of Elvis's show, a friend of Buddy and Bob, added them to the bill, and Holly became friendly enough with Elvis to hang out with him regularly when Elvis passed through town in those early career years. "But it wasn't until he saw Elvis live in 1955 that Buddy Holly knew he didn't want to do anything, or that they become a rock and roll star."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Purchase of Fender Stratocaster (1955)
podcast.body: Believing in Buddy's talent, bass player Larry Wellborn lent him $1000 in 1955—a substantial sum at the time—which enabled Holly to purchase his first Fender Stratocaster, an amplifier, and a stage suit, marking a significant investment in his rock and roll career. "Larry Wellborne, believed in Buddy's talent and lent him $1000, a massive amount of money in 1955, so he could buy himself a friend of Stratocaster, an amp, and a stage suit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: The Stratocaster's "Gear Shift" (1955)
podcast.body: Holly's friend Joe B. Mauldin humorously described the Fender Stratocaster as the first instrument he'd ever seen with a "gear shift," referring to its innovative tremolo arm, which had only been introduced that year. "Holly's friend Joe B. Mouldin said of the Strat that it was the first instrument he'd ever seen with a gear shift."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Decca Records Misspells Name (1956)
podcast.body: When signing his paperwork for Decca Records, Charles Holley (H-O-L-L-E-Y) discovered his name was misspelled as H-O-L-L-Y. Told they needed the document back quickly, he signed it, and from then on, he was known as Buddy Holly, without the 'e'. "When the paperwork for it came through for Buddy to sign, he discovered that they'd miss spelled his name."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Decca's Disillusionment (1956)
podcast.body: Throughout 1956, Decca Records grew increasingly disillusioned with Buddy Holly's lack of commercial success, despite numerous recordings. Paul Cohen, the executive who signed Holly, was known to tell friends that Buddy Holly was "the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with." "Decker became ever more disillusioned with Holly, while Paul Cohen, the executive at Decker who had signed Holly, at one point was telling his friends, Buddy Holly is the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Early Recordings at Owen Bradley's Studio (Pre-1956)
podcast.body: Owen Bradley's studio in Nashville, where Gene Vincent's initial recording session took place, had very recently hosted Buddy Holly. This studio had recorded some of the early tracks for the singer from Texas, indicating its role in fostering emerging talent. "The session was at a studio run by Owen Bradley, who had just recently recorded some early tracks by a singer from Texas named Buddy Holly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: End of 1956 Career Stagnation
podcast.body: As 1956 drew to a close, Buddy Holly found himself in a difficult position: without his long-time guitarist Sonny Curtis, signed to a record company that did not know how to promote him, and failing to realize his musical ambitions despite constant recording. "So as 1956 drew to a close, Buddy Holly was without his long-time guitarist, signed to a record company that didn't know what to do with him, and failing to realise his musical ambitions."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Failed Louisiana Hayride Attempt (1956)
podcast.body: Elvis had assured Buddy Holly that the Louisiana Hayride would feature him based on his recommendation. However, when Holly and Sonny Curtis drove to Shreveport, the radio station informed them that Elvis did not control their bookings, forcing them to return to Texas without performing. "Elvis had told him that the Louisiana Hayride would definitely have him on at Elvis's recommendation, but when he and Sonny Curtis drove to Shreveport, the radio station told him that it wasn't up to Elvis who got on their show and who didn't."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Meeting Peggy Sue Gehrman (1956)
podcast.body: Buddy Holly did not meet Peggy Sue Gehrman, the woman who inspired the song "Peggy Sue," until 1956. "Buddy Holly didn't meet Peggy Sue Gehrman, the woman who gave the song its name, until 1956."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 48: "Rock With the Caveman" by Tommy Steele

podcast.title: Anxiety Over Chart Success (1957)
podcast.body: During a fishing holiday in Colorado, Holly was constantly worried about the lack of success of "That'll Be the Day" and obsessed over Paul Anka's number one hit "Diana," feeling his own records were just as good. "But he spent much of the trip worried about the lack of success of that'll be the day, and obsessing over a new record by a new singer, Paul Hanke, that had gone to number one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Decca Contract Prevents Re-recording (1957)
podcast.body: Following the expiration of his Decca contract, Buddy Holly was prohibited from re-recording any songs he had recorded for the label in 1956 for a period of five years, a clause that significantly complicated his future recording plans. "Buddy's contract with Decker said that even though they'd only released two singles by him and hadn't bothered to release any of the other songs he'd recorded during the year he was signed to them, he couldn't re-record anything he'd recorded for them for another five years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Early Career Stagnation (1957)
podcast.body: Despite an astonishing outpouring of songs, including "Everyday," "Not Fade Away," and covers of Fats Domino and Little Richard, Holly and The Crickets recorded extensively before having a single hit with "That'll Be the Day" or "Words of Love." "Remember, this was all before they'd had a single hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Harlem Apollo Performance (1957)
podcast.body: When The Crickets performed at the notoriously hostile Harlem Apollo, they had to reconfigure their sets because the audience disliked Holly's original material, with the exception of "That'll Be the Day," but responded well to their R&B cover versions like Bo Diddley. They worked hard to win over the audience. "the group had to reconfigure their sets, as the audiences didn't like any of Holly's original material, except that'll be the day."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Limited Touring History (Pre-1957)
podcast.body: According to the Buddy Holly Centre in Lubbock, Texas, Buddy Holly did not perform outside Lubbock until a Grand Ole Opry tour in May 1956, and only performed outside West Texas one other time before 1957. "Holly didn't perform outside Lubbock until that tour, and that's the only time he did perform outside West Texas until 1957."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 48: "Rock With the Caveman" by Tommy Steele

podcast.title: Plane Crash Death (1957)
podcast.body: On February 3, 1957, a day famously known as "the day the music died," Buddy Holly was killed when the small plane he was a passenger in went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa. He died alongside fellow musicians Richie Valens and The Big Bopper. "February 3rd, 1957 has gone down in history as the day the music died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: Racial Ambiguity in Early Success (1957)
podcast.body: "That'll Be the Day" gained traction after Black radio stations began playing it, mistaking The Crickets for an earlier Black doo-wop group also called The Crickets. This led to the band being booked on an otherwise all-Black tour without the promoters realizing they were white. "People at Black radio stations had assumed that this new group called the Crickets was the same one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Creative Explosion in Greenwich Village (1958)
podcast.body: After firing Norman Petty and being cut off financially, Holly moved to Greenwich Village with Maria Elena and experienced a massive creative surge, writing dozens of acoustic demos and planning ambitious projects including a Latin music album, gospel duets with Mahalia Jackson, and soul duets with Ray Charles. He also enrolled in Lee Strasberg's Actor's Studio to study method acting. "He was not only writing songs himself, but he was busily planning to make an album of Latin music, and he was making preparations for two more projects he'd like to do. An album of duets on gospel songs with Mahalia Jackson, and an album of sold duets with Ray Charles."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Petty's Contract Deception (1958)
podcast.body: Norman Petty revealed that Holly had actually been recording for Petty's company, not Brunswick or Coral, meaning all royalties went to Petty, and the Crickets' supposed bank account was empty. This financial revelation occurred while Maria Elena was pregnant, forcing Holly to undertake the "Winter Dance Party" tour. "By the terms of buddy's contract, he hadn't really been recording for Buns Recall Coral, so they didn't tell him a penny."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Maria Elena's Tragic Discovery and Miscarriage (1959)
podcast.body: Maria Elena learned of Buddy Holly's death from the television, not the police, which later prompted changes in how news of celebrity deaths was handled. She was so distraught that she miscarried two days later and has never been able to visit his grave. "Maria Elena found out about Bodies Death, not from the police, but from the TV."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Plane Crash Circumstances (1959)
podcast.body: After a show in Clear Lake, Iowa, Holly chartered a plane to Fargo, North Dakota, to get laundry done and sleep in a real bed. Tommy Allsup and Waylon Jennings gave up their seats to the Big Bopper and Richie Valens, who were suffering the most from the tour conditions. The pilot, despite being good in daylight, had a poor instrument flight rating, and the plane had an unusual altimeter that functioned inversely to typical models. The plane plummeted nose first less than five minutes after takeoff, killing everyone instantly. "The plane took off, and less than five minutes after takeoff, it plummeted straight down, nose first, into the ground top speed, killing everyone on board instantly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Plane Crash Death (1959)
podcast.body: Buddy Holly was killed in a small plane crash in a cornfield outside Mason City, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. This tragedy, which also claimed the lives of Ritchie Valens and Big Wopper, is historically referred to as "the day the music died." "Buddy Holly, Richie Val, and Big Wopper were all killed when their small plane went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa."

podcast.title: Posthumous Financial Success for Petty (1959-1965)
podcast.body: After Holly's death, Norman Petty profited immensely from a stockpile of unreleased Buddy Holly recordings. He also secured an agreement with Holly's estate to overdub new backing tracks onto Holly's acoustic demos, transforming them into full-band rock and roll songs, which resulted in posthumous hit singles until 1965 outside the US, making both Petty and Holly's estate wealthy. "Suddenly, his stockpile of unreleased Buddy Holly recordings was a gold mine, and not only that, he ended up coming to an agreement with Holly's estate that he could take all those demos Holly had recorded, and overdub new backing tracks on them, turning them into full-blown rock-and-roll songs."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Robert Zimmerman's Early Exposure (1959)
podcast.body: A young man named Robert Zimmerman, later known as Bob Dylan, saw one of the Winter Dance Party shows in Duluth, Minnesota, where Holly, Dion, and Valens were taking turns playing drums due to their drummer's frostbite. "The shows were still good, at least according to a young man named Robert Zimmerman, who saw the first drummers show in Duluth, Minnesota."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: The Winter Dance Party Tour Conditions (1959)
podcast.body: The tour in Wisconsin, Iowa, and Minnesota through January and February 1959 was plagued by miserable conditions, including zigzagging routes with 400-mile distances between gigs, musicians sleeping on buses, and using eight different buses in 11 days due to breakdowns. Heating failures in temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit and three feet of snow caused illness (flu for Bopper and Valens) and frostbite (Carl Bunch). "The musicians had to sleep on the tour bus, or buses."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Songs Acquired by Paul McCartney (1973)
podcast.body: Many of Buddy Holly's songs were part of the Norvat Jack Music company, which Paul McCartney acquired in 1973. Buddy Holly was described as one of McCartney's idols. "Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly, one of McCartney's idols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer

podcast.title: Posthumous Hologram Tour (2018)
podcast.body: Despite having passed away in 1959, Buddy Holly embarked on a hologram tour in 2018. This tour, along with similar ventures for other deceased artists, showcased the advancements in projection technology that allowed lifelike 3D images to appear on stage, marking a new era for posthumous performances. "In 2018, Buddy Holly, dead since 1959, and Roy Orbison, dead since 1988, were on stage again as holograms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Admiration for Mickey & Sylvia
podcast.body: Buddy Holly, early in his career, was a significant fan of Mickey & Sylvia's music. He imitated Sylvia's vocal style, particularly her way of singing "Baby," in many of his own records. "You can tell how much Holly liked Mickey and Sylvia though, just by comparing the way he sings Baby on many of his records, so the way Sylvia sings it in Lovey's Strange."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Affair and Group Tensions (Year not specified)
podcast.body: Holly was secretly having an affair with a married woman, which caused tension as his best friend and bandmate, Jerry Allison, was also in love with her. This personal conflict, along with Nikki Sullivan's growing unhappiness, contributed to internal group problems. "Holly was having an affair with a married woman at the time, and Jerry Allison, who was Holly's best friend as well as his bandmate, was also in love with her, though not in a relationship with her, and so Holly had to keep his affair hidden from his best friend."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Appearance on Alan Freed Tour
podcast.body: Buddy Holly was one of the eleven acts, alongside Chuck Berry, Larry Williams, The Chantels, and Jerry Lee Lewis, on the legendary Alan Freed tour. "It was around this time that Jerry Lee went on the Alan Fried tour that we mentioned last week, with Chuck Berry, Buddy Holly, Larry Williams, the Chantel's, and Eleven Other Act."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Backstage Revelations at Brooklyn Paramount (Year not specified)
podcast.body: During an engagement at the Brooklyn Paramount on an Alan Fried show, Nikki Sullivan, while trying to quit smoking and in a bad mood, revealed Holly's affair to Jerry Allison, leading to a fist fight within the group. "Nikki Sullivan, who was in an awful mood because he was trying to quit smoking, revealed the truth about Holly's affair to Alison, and the group got in a fist fight."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Collaborator with Grady Martin
podcast.body: Buddy Holly is mentioned as one of the artists for whom session guitarist Grady Martin played on recordings. "Grady was a session guitarist in Nashville who played on hundreds of recordings for people like Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and even Buddy Holly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Cover of "Honky Tonk"
podcast.body: Buddy Holly, an artist not typically associated with instrumental R&B, recorded a cover version of Bill Doggett's "Honky Tonk," showcasing the song's broad appeal across genres and artists. "But by other people you might not expect, like Buddy Holly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 50: "Honky Tonk", by Bill Doggett

podcast.title: Early Musical Background
podcast.body: Holly grew up in Lubbock, Texas, a town notable for producing many famous musicians. His elder brothers performed as a country duo, modeling their style after the Louvin Brothers, influencing Holly's early exposure to music. "Holly grew up with music. His elder brothers performed as a country duo in much the same style as the Louvain Brothers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Early Singer-Songwriter
podcast.body: Buddy Holly was an early example of a performer who both wrote and sang their own songs, contributing to a higher output of music. "But then came along people who could do both. Buddy Holly, Bob Dylan, the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Financial Exploitation by Norman Petty (Year not specified)
podcast.body: Despite promises of an equal share of income, producer and manager Norman Petty began to manipulate the group's finances, handling all the money himself and only giving the members pocket money. He eventually reconfigured the live act's financial split, giving Holly 50% and Mauldin/Allison 25% each, while keeping the full amount himself. "Petty was handling all the money and only giving the group pocket money, rather than giving them their actual shares of the money they'd earned."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Halo Claim
podcast.body: Dylan later claimed to have seen a halo over Buddy Holly's head during the performance he attended. "He later claimed to have seen a halo over Holly's head during the performance."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Hologram Tour (Current)
podcast.body: Buddy Holly's image is currently used in hologram tours, where an actor's image is projected onto glass using the Pepper's Ghost trick, accompanied by a live band playing along to his records, continuing to generate income for his estate. "You can now go and see a hologram tour, in which an image of a look not very alike actor is projected on glass, using the old Victorian stage trick Peppers Ghost, while a live band plays along to the records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Iconic Stratocaster Use
podcast.body: Buddy Holly is frequently depicted holding a Fender Stratocaster in photographs, indicating his prominent use of the instrument and its association with his image. "Pretty much every picture I've seen a buddy Holly holding a guitar as him holding a Strat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Ill-fated Tour
podcast.body: Buddy Holly was part of an ill-fated tour, on the penultimate date of which he performed for a young Robert Zimmerman (Bob Dylan), alongside Richie Valens and The Big Bopper. "He was enough of a fan of Rock and Roll music that he went to see Buddy Holly, Richie Valens, and the Big Bopper, on the penultimate date of their ill-fated tour."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Inaccurate Inspiration for Tommy Steele
podcast.body: Tommy Steele claimed to have been introduced to rock and roll by seeing Buddy Holly sing "Peggy Sue" on a Grand Ole Opry tour in Norfolk, Virginia, in 1955. This account is contradicted by various timelines, including those from the Buddy Holly Centre in Lubbock, Texas, which indicate Holly did not tour outside Lubbock until May 1956, never toured Virginia, and "Peggy Sue" was written in 1957. "So, whatever it was that introduced young Tommy Hicks to the wonders of rock and roll, it wasn't seeing Buddy Holly sing Peggy Sue in North of Virginia in 1955."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 48: "Rock With the Caveman" by Tommy Steele

podcast.title: Iowa Plane Crash Fatality
podcast.body: Buddy Holly died early in 1959 in an infamous Iowa plane crash, along with J.P. Richardson (The Big Bopper) and Ritchie Valens. "that also took the lives of Buddy Holly and Richie Valens."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 2 - Countryish Music of the 1970s (Encore)

podcast.title: Joe Meek's Obsession
podcast.body: Joe Meek developed an intense and profound obsession with Buddy Holly, who had tragically died in a plane crash. Meek claimed to communicate with Holly in his dreams, a detail that further underscores Meek's deep fascination with the occult and the afterlife. "Además, estaba obsesionado con Badi Holly, que n' había muerto en un accidente de avión, decía que se comunicaba con el ensueños."

xref.title: Plane Crash Death (1957)
xref.body: On February 3, 1957, a day famously known as "the day the music died," Richie Valens was killed when the small plane he was a passenger in went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa. He died alongside fellow musicians Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper. "February 3rd, 1957 has gone down in history as the day the music died."

xref.title: 1958 Percy Phillips Home Recording – "That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger"
xref.body: An ultra-rare, two-sided 78 RPM disc from 1958, recorded by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, pianist John Lowe, and drummer Colin Hanton at the home of Percy Phillips, who specialized in "down and dirty" recordings in his front room. Side one features Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day," and side two contains "In Spite of All the Danger," the first-ever Lennon-McCartney recording. This record is owned by Paul McCartney and is estimated to be worth at least 100,000 pounds if it were ever to be sold. "The result was a two-sided 78 RPM disc with Buddy Holly's That'll Be the Day on Side One, and the first ever Lennon McCartney recording on the other, in spite of all the danger."

xref.title: Lyric and Tempo Evolution
xref.body: "Buddy Holly" underwent several changes during its production. Early demos contained rap slang that was later removed. The lyrics initially referred to Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire but eventually morphed into Mary Tyler Moore and Buddy Holly. Furthermore, the song's tempo was increased in the studio and further tweaked to a higher pace during the mastering process. "Instead of the lyrics referring to Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire, they morphed into Mary Tyler Moore and Buddy Holly."

xref.body: Paul McCartney possesses the singular original recording of Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day" by his pre-Beatles band, The Quarrymen, with its estimated value being around $250,000 US. "Paul McCartney owns the one and only original copy, and its estimated value is in the vicinity of 250,000 US."

xref.title: Paul McCartney's Shock and Subsequent Catalog Acquisitions
xref.body: Paul McCartney was "especially stunned" by the loss of his Beatles' publishing rights. This experience motivated him to invest heavily in music catalogs, beginning in 1973 with the purchase of Norvat Jack Music, which included songs by his idol Buddy Holly, establishing a significant income stream from controlled catalogs. "Paul McCartney was especially stunned by this. He learned the hard way about the value of owning the publishing-depository music. So if he couldn't own his own music, the music he made with the Beatles, he decided that he would bulk up his financial holdings by buying the catalogs of others. He started in 1973 buying a company called Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly"

xref.title: Posthumous Impact and Legacy
xref.body: After his death, Kurt's image elevated him to the status of icons like Elvis, Buddy Holly, John Lennon, and Tupac, profoundly influencing rock, pop, and even hip-hop through his music, attitude, and image. "From that point on, Kurt was up there with Elvis, and Buddy Holly, and John Lennon, and Tupac."

xref.title: Producer Ric Ocasek's Persuasion
xref.body: Despite Rivers Cuomo's strong reservations, producer Ric Ocasek, leader of The Cars, was adamant about including "Buddy Holly" on the debut album. He, along with the other band members, insisted on its inclusion. Ocasek eventually convinced Cuomo by suggesting they record it, and if Cuomo still disliked it, they could leave it off, but warning him it would be "stupid not to include it." "But Rico Kasek, the leader of the cars and the guy tapped to produce the record, would have none of that."

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Friendship with King He
xref.body: The song "Buddy Holly" was a direct result of Rivers Cuomo's protectiveness over his Korean friend, King He. Cuomo became "really pissed off" when other band members made fun of her, recalling how she was often picked on in high school. The song was written as an expression of his commitment to their platonic relationship and his readiness to defend her. "It's about a particular girl I knew."

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Initial Rejection of "Buddy Holly"
xref.body: Rivers Cuomo initially refused to consider including "Buddy Holly" on Weezer's debut album, deeming it "too cheesy" and an outlier compared to his other compositions. He felt it didn't fit the band's intended sound. "For the longest time, he refused to consider including the song and Weezer's debut album because it was too cheesy."

xref.title: Session Guitarist on Iconic Recordings
xref.body: Grady Martin was a prolific session guitarist in Nashville, contributing to hundreds of recordings for prominent artists such as Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, and Buddy Holly. His work as a session musician placed him at the heart of many significant musical developments. "Grady was a session guitarist in Nashville who played on hundreds of recordings for people like Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and even Buddy Holly."

xref.title: Songwriting Process on Santa Monica College Campus
xref.body: Rivers Cuomo developed the lyrics for "Buddy Holly" while walking through the campus of Santa Monica College, where both he and King He were attending school. The iconic line "weew, I look just like Buddy Holly" was conceived at the same speed as his walking pace, indicating an organic, real-time inspiration. "He came up with the lyrics while walking through the campus of Santa Monica College where he and King He were attending school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio Dynamics and "Buddy Holly" Notes
xref.body: During the recording sessions for Weezer's debut album, notes reading "weew, what, Buddy Holly" began to appear around the studio. This suggests the other band members and producer Ric Ocasek were playfully but persistently advocating for the song's inclusion, despite Rivers Cuomo's initial reluctance. "Little notes started appearing around the studio that said, weew, what, Buddy Holly."
